title: Addas and the grapes
hookLine: a Christian servant from Nineveh brings him grapes and hears him speak of Yunus (sirah)
last: IF YOU'RE NOT ANGRY, I DON'T MIND.

cards: Two brothers own the orchard where he's resting: Utba and Shayba, sons of Rabi'a, men of Quraysh who are no friends of his message. They've watched what Ta'if did to him, and something in them moves.
Ibn Ishaq says they felt for him as a kinsman. They call their servant, a Christian man named Addas: take a bunch of these grapes on a plate to that man, and tell him to eat. Today: Addas.

teach.b: Addas sets the grapes down. The Prophet reaches out, and before he eats, he says, in the name of Allah. Addas looks at him.
These are not words, he says, that the people of this country say.
So the Prophet asks him: where are you from, Addas, and what is your religion? A Christian, Addas says, from Nineveh.
And the Prophet answers: from the town of the righteous man Yunus, son of Matta. Addas is astonished. How do you know who Yunus son of Matta was?
In Ibn Ishaq's account the Prophet says: he is my brother. He was a prophet, and I am a prophet. And Addas bends over him and kisses his head, his hands and his feet.
By the wall, one brother says to the other: well, he's spoiled your servant for you.

When Addas comes back they scold him, and he answers that there is nothing on earth better than this man; he told me something only a prophet would know. Look at who meets here. A man just driven out by his own kind.
A servant far from home, in a town where nobody says what he says. And between them, a name both of them know: Yunus, whom the Qur'an remembers as one of the messengers, the man of the fish.
Christians and Jews tell his story too, as Jonah. What opens the door is not an argument.
It's a plate of grapes, two words said before eating, and a question about where someone comes from. And notice who sent the grapes: two men who did not share his faith.

how: Muslims retell the meeting with Addas as part of the Ta'if story, and say bismillah, in the name of Allah, before eating.

o: a prophet of Nineveh, also called Jonah
a Christian servant from Nineveh who brought grapes
the orchard owner who drove him from Ta'if

games.q: Addas and the grapes — tap the pairs.

s: the grapes were sent by his followers
Utba and Shayba, men of Quraysh, sent them, feeling for him as a kinsman.
Addas noticed the words he said before eating
these aren't words the people of this country say, he told him.
Yunus is remembered in the Qur'an as one of the messengers
the sirah ties him to Nineveh; Christians and Jews know him as Jonah.

games.q: you're Addas. a stranger says Allah's name over the grapes you brought, and then names your hometown's prophet. what do you do?
o: leave the plate and go back.
ask how he knows of Yunus.
games.why: Addas asked how he knew; when he heard 'he is my brother, a prophet', he kissed his head, hands and feet.

practice: Think through your week for one person who is running on empty: a coworker on a double shift, a parent with a newborn, someone far from home.

Picture something small and real you could bring them, a piece of fruit, a cup of tea, and one question you could ask, the way he asked Addas where he was from. If you pray, you can say bismillah before you next eat.

wordCard.voice: Addas. A Christian servant from Nineveh who carries grapes to a rejected man, hears him say Allah's name and speak of Yunus, and kisses his hands. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: grapes; the fruit Addas carried on the plate.

carryVoice: Your line: a bowl of grapes. A servant far from home, and a name both men knew. Until tomorrow.
